analysis.one_liner: Stops police and intelligence agencies from buying Americans' location and phone records from data brokers without a court order.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 219-199 on April 17, 2024, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, government agencies can get around the warrant requirement by simply buying your location history, phone records, or online data from companies that collect and sell it. This bill would make it illegal for law enforcement and intelligence agencies to purchase those records, bar other agencies from sharing bought data with them, and require a court order before any such data can be demanded from a company. It also extends existing privacy rules for phone and internet providers to the middleman companies that handle communications behind the scenes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose location, communications, and online records are currently collected and sold to government agencies without a warrant. The bill would close that loophole: agencies could no longer buy their way around the Fourth Amendment, purchased data could not be used against you in court, and intelligence agencies would have to use the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act's court-based processes to get location, web browsing, and search history of people in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone with a phone or online account

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits law enforcement and intelligence agencies from obtaining covered customer or subscriber records — including communications contents, location information, and device data — from a third party in exchange for anything of value, and closes workarounds by applying the ban no matter which middleman holds the data.
Bars other government agencies from sharing purchased records with law enforcement or intelligence agencies, and makes any such records and evidence derived from them inadmissible in court.

Requires the government to get a court order, judged by the most stringent applicable standard, before compelling a third party to hand over these records or 'illegitimately obtained' information such as data taken by deceiving users or violating a platform's terms.

Extends the Stored Communications Act's bans on divulging the contents of stored communications to intermediary service providers — the companies that deliver, store, or process communications for phone and internet providers.

Makes FISA the exclusive legal channel for acquiring location information, web browsing history, and internet search history of people inside the United States for foreign intelligence purposes, and requires Attorney General minimization procedures for data acquired in violation of the ban.

analysis.who_pays: The data broker industry, which loses a paying government customer base; and law enforcement and intelligence agencies, which lose a convenient shortcut to records they could otherwise buy without going to a judge. Investigators would have to meet the same legal standards that already apply to phone and internet providers.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves significant carve-outs: records people made public on social media, public government records, background-check data obtained with written consent, and data generated by automated license plate recognition systems are all excluded from the prohibition, so police could still obtain much information without a warrant.
Law enforcement agencies would lose a tool they currently use in investigations; gathering the same records would now require going to a court, which agencies argue slows time-sensitive cases.

The exclusive-means provisions in Section 5 also narrow how intelligence agencies can acquire some communications records and location data even outside the broker-purchase context, which supporters of broader surveillance authority opposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending a practice that lets agencies buy the kind of data they would need a warrant to demand — is substantial and squarely a Fourth Amendment protection. The cost is real but modest: investigators and intelligence agencies would have to use existing court processes, and the bill itself contains carve-outs (license plate data, public posts, background checks) that blunt the objections. The main design weakness is that the exemptions leave much data fair game.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 219-199, but the Senate received it and never voted on it, so it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH) with 7 bipartisan cosponsors on July 14, 2023.

The House Judiciary Committee marked it up and ordered it reported by a 30-0 vote on July 19, 2023, and reported it in April 2024; the Intelligence Committee was discharged from further consideration.
The House debated it under a structured rule and passed it on April 17, 2024, by a vote of 219-199 with 1 member voting present.
The Senate received the bill on April 18, 2024, and took no further action; no Senate committee or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the law enforcement and intelligence agencies that buy their data came out ahead: the loophole the bill would have closed stayed open, and no court order is required to buy most of these records. People whose location and communications data is sold to the government lost the chance at that protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and agencies that buy their data

industries.note: The bill bans agencies from buying covered customer records — including location data and communications records — in exchange for anything of value, eliminating a paying government market for brokered personal data. Brokers profit from selling data that agencies would otherwise need a court order to demand directly.

Section 5 makes FISA the exclusive means for acquiring location, web browsing, and search history of people in the United States for foreign intelligence purposes, and the bill makes purchased or 'illegitimately obtained' data inadmissible in court. This forecloses acquisition channels the intelligence community currently uses.

The bill explicitly exempts data generated by ALPR systems from its prohibitions, so police can continue obtaining license-plate location data from these systems without a court order even as other broker purchases are banned.

The bill extends Stored Communications Act disclosure bans to intermediary service providers that deliver, store, or process communications for phone and internet companies, adding compliance restrictions. These same rules protect customers' communications from government access.
